Where is Hinds County and how is it laid out?

Hinds County sits in central Mississippi and is the state's most populous county, with 227,742 residents at the 2020 census. It covers 877 square miles, of which 870 are land, and it has two county seats: Jackson and Raymond.

That two-seat arrangement shapes almost every property tax errand. The county is split into a First Judicial District (Jackson) and a Second Judicial District (Raymond), and the tax collector, tax assessor and chancery clerk each keep an office in both places.

The cities are Byram, Clinton, Jackson and Raymond. The towns are Bolton, Edwards, Learned, Terry and Utica, and unincorporated places such as Brownsville, Cayuga, Cynthia, Midway, Oakley and Pocahontas fill in the rural parts. Part of Jackson lies in Madison and Rankin counties, so check which county bills a given parcel.

Interstates 20, 55 and 220 cross the county, along with US 49, US 51 and US 80, and a stretch of the Natchez Trace Parkway runs through it. Public-use airports are Hawkins Field in Jackson and John Bell Williams Airport in Raymond.

Which Hinds County offices handle property tax?

Three elected offices share the work: the tax assessor values property, the tax collector sends bills and takes payment, and the chancery clerk records deeds, runs the appeal hearing process through the Board of Supervisors, and collects delinquent taxes. Each has a Jackson and a Raymond location, open 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Monday through Friday except legal holidays.

The numbers above come from the county's own office pages and can change, so call before you drive.

You can read each office's page on the county site: Tax Collector, Tax Assessor and Chancery Clerk.

How does the Hinds County assessor value a house?

The assessor lists every taxable parcel, estimates its value, applies the state assessment ratio and certifies a roll to the Board of Supervisors. The office says its territory runs from Learned, with about 100 parcels, up to the City of Jackson, with more than 70,000, and totals over 106,000 parcels.

Under the state's classes, a single-family, owner-occupied home is Class I and is assessed at 10 percent of true value. Other real estate, such as a rental house, is Class II at 15 percent. The Mississippi Department of Revenue explains that taxes equal true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate.

Hinds County says it reviews 25 percent of taxable property each year, so every parcel is looked at at least once every four years. For most houses that means a drive-by comparison against the drawings and field sheet in the office. The assessor only contacts an owner if what the appraiser sees differs from the file. The state adds that interior inspections of homes are not required.

The office also runs sales ratio studies, comparing appraised values with actual sale prices, and the State Tax Commission does its own.

  • Ownership is set as of January 1 using deeds filed with the chancery clerk.
  • The assessment roll goes to the Board of Supervisors on the first Monday in July.
  • The office's past policy has been to notify owners when a new appraisal rises $2,000 or more over the prior year.

What dates matter on a Hinds County tax bill?

Taxes are due on or before February 1 for property assessed the previous year, and if February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday, payment is accepted the next Monday without penalty. The chancery clerk's office says statements are mailed from the tax collector each December and that current taxes may be paid in three installments.

After February 1, state law adds interest of one-half of one percent per month, or fraction of a month, on unpaid tax. The governor can extend that date by proclamation for unusual conditions, for up to 60 days at a time.

How do I appeal a Hinds County assessment?

You ask the county Board of Supervisors for a hearing, and the Chancery Clerk is the contact for that request. The state says an appeal normally has to be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax comes due.

Start earlier, though. The Hinds assessor says its office will review values with an owner at any time of year, and its page describes the formal appeal as the next step under Mississippi Code 27-35-89. For business personal property, the office posts values after the first Monday in July, offers review through July 31, and says a formal protest must reach the chancery clerk by 9:00 a.m. on the first Monday in August.

Bring evidence about value. Lafayette County's appeal guide says boards weigh the fairness and accuracy of the value and that a recent appraisal of your own house is the best exhibit. Hinds has not published matching guidance we could confirm, but the same logic applies.

If an appraisal has the wrong square footage, the state says you may sometimes get a refund for prior years through the chancery clerk.

What happens if Hinds County taxes go unpaid?

The house goes to the county tax sale on the last Monday in August, and if nobody bids, it is struck off to the state. The chancery clerk collects delinquent taxes, and once a year is delinquent the clerk says the older years must be cleared before the current year can be paid.

The clerk's page lists some firm rules for delinquent payments: no installments, and payment by cash or money order only, with no personal checks. The owner has two years from the sale date to redeem. If the two years pass, the property either matures to the state or the buyer receives a tax deed, which the clerk's own page describes as meaning you no longer own the property.

The state also publishes a Secretary of State line, 1-866-835-2637, for property that was sold to the state. Hinds posts delinquent and tax sale lists on its county site.

  • Redemption means paying the delinquent taxes plus statutory damages and interest, as Mississippi courts have described it.
  • An owner who sells before the sale date can clear the taxes from the sale proceeds.
  • An owner who waits until after the sale can still redeem, but only through the chancery clerk.

Selling a Hinds County house when property tax is still owed

You can sell a house with unpaid taxes, because taxes are cleared through the title and closing process. A title search turns up any back taxes, mortgages or other liens, and the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

The chancery clerk's guidance for buyers is useful for sellers too. A title search should be done before any money changes hands, and any attorney or title company can do it. The clerk's office itself may not search the records or prepare a deed. A deed must carry the seller's notarized signature, a legal description with indexing instructions, and the names, addresses and phone numbers of the sellers, buyers and preparer.

Timing matters if the house is occupied by an owner. The clerk notes that a buyer who occupies the home before January 1 can apply for homestead exemption from January 1 to April 1, which lowers that year's tax. A cash sale to an investor generally does not change the sequence, because the recording and tax steps are the same. It mainly removes the wait for a buyer's lender.

Sellers in Hinds County often arrive with older homes, inherited houses or rentals. Probate and heirship questions go to the chancery court, which hears probate and land matters, and the clerk's office files those papers. If the owner has died, clearing title may need to happen before a deed can be signed.

What should Hinds County sellers know about the local market around them?

Hinds County's economy leans on government, health care and education centered in Jackson. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Hinds County employment of 109,600 in December 2024, the highest of any Mississippi county. The University of Mississippi Medical Center, based in Jackson, says it has more than 10,000 full- and part-time employees.

Public schools are served by three districts: Jackson Public School District, Clinton Public School District and Hinds County School District. State-run schools for the blind and the deaf are also in the county. Colleges include Jackson State University, Millsaps College, Belhaven University, Mississippi College in Clinton and Hinds Community College in Raymond.

Population has been falling. The Census Bureau counted 250,998 people in 1980 and 227,742 in 2020, and estimates 211,888 for 2025. For a seller, that trend can mean fewer buyers per listing, and a clean tax record removes one obstacle to closing.

When are Hinds County property taxes due?

Taxes are due on or before February 1 for the previous assessment year. If that date falls on a weekend or legal holiday, you have until the next Monday without penalty or interest. After that, interest of one-half of one percent per month applies.

Where do I pay property tax in Hinds County?

You pay the Hinds County Tax Collector, which has offices at 316 S. President St. in Jackson and 127 W. Main St. in Raymond. The office accepts cash, check or credit card with a 2.25 percent surcharge, and tags paid by personal check are held for 10 working days.

What is the Hinds County assessment ratio for a home?

An owner-occupied single-family home is assessed at 10 percent of true value, and other real property such as a rental is assessed at 15 percent. The assessed value is then multiplied by the combined millage rate of the county, city and school district.

What is the deadline to appeal a Hinds County property assessment?

Normally the first Monday in August before the tax is due. You request a hearing with the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk, so start with the assessor well before that date.

Can I sell my Hinds County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the back taxes from your proceeds at closing. If the house has already gone to tax sale, the chancery clerk collects the redemption amount, and the owner has two years from the sale date to redeem.

Where is DeSoto County, Mississippi, and how is it laid out?

DeSoto County sits in the northwest corner of Mississippi, directly south of Shelby County, Tennessee, and its county seat is Hernando. The county covers 497 square miles, of which 476 are land, and it borders Crittenden County, Arkansas, to the west across the Mississippi River, plus Tunica, Tate and Marshall counties.

Most people live in four cities: Hernando, Horn Lake, Olive Branch and Southaven. The county also has one town, Walls, several census-designated places such as Lake View, Lynchburg and Pleasant Hill, and unincorporated communities like Lake Cormorant, Nesbit and Cockrum. Where a house sits decides which city or school levy shows up on the bill, so the first step for any seller is to look at the parcel's tax district.

How did DeSoto County grow into a Memphis suburb?

The county was organized in 1836 and farmed cotton first, then dairy and soybeans, before subdivisions replaced the fields. According to a county history on the county website, soybean acreage passed cotton by 1970, and by 1999 only three dairies were left.

The same history marks the turning points that built the housing stock you see today:

  • Homes in the Southaven community went on sale in 1958, and the city was incorporated on March 25, 1980.
  • Interstate 55 opened through Hernando in 1964.
  • New one-family homes ran above 1,000 a year in the early 1970s.
  • The county's population was 67,910 in 1990, according to the 1990 census, and the Wikipedia table of census counts shows 107,199 in 2000 and 161,252 in 2010.

For a seller this means DeSoto County houses span several building eras. A 1970s ranch in Horn Lake and a 2010s two-story in Olive Branch will face very different repair lists, even though both are billed by the same collector.

What do roads and schools mean for a DeSoto County house?

Four routes carry most traffic: Interstate 55, Interstate 69, Interstate 269, plus U.S. 51 and U.S. 61. The county has no fixed-route transit of its own. Memphis Area Transit Authority, Amtrak, Greyhound and other carriers serve nearby Memphis instead, so most households depend on a car.

Public education is run by one district, the DeSoto County School District, which covers the whole county and is the largest in the state. That keeps school boundaries simple compared with counties that split among several districts, although attendance zones still differ by address.

Who assesses and who collects property tax in DeSoto County?

The Tax Assessor values the property and the Tax Collector bills and collects it. Both offices are in Hernando. The county lists the Tax Collector at 365 Losher Street, Suite 110, Hernando, phone 662-469-8030, with a second office on BJ Chain Drive in Olive Branch. A city notice from Hernando places the Tax Assessor at 365 Losher Street, Suite 100, and the county homestead page gives the assessor's phone as 662-469-8029.

Under state law the assessor must revalue real property at least once every four years, and taxable personal property every year. Interior inspections of homes are not required, according to the Mississippi Department of Revenue. Voters do not set your rate directly. The county, the city and the school district each decide what they need, and local officials turn that into a millage rate.

The state formula is true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate. A rental house in DeSoto County lands in Class II, so it is assessed at a higher share of value than an owner-occupied home, before millage is applied.

When are DeSoto County property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?

Mississippi property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1, bills go out in November and December, and the tax is due by February 1. If February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday, the Department of Revenue says payment is accepted the following Monday without penalty or interest. DeSoto County's own audited financial statements say taxes on real and personal property are due on or before February 1 of the following year.

If real estate taxes stay unpaid, the parcel can go to the county tax sale. The state says some counties hold that sale on the first Monday in April and others on the last Monday in August, so confirm the date with the collector.

  • A buyer who purchases at a tax sale does not take clear title right away. The owner can redeem within two years of the sale, according to Mississippi Supreme Court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3.
  • If nobody buys the parcel at the sale, it goes to the State of Mississippi and is handled by the Secretary of State, phone 1-866-835-2637.
  • Delinquent taxes are a lien problem for a sale. A title company will want them paid at closing.

How do I appeal a DeSoto County assessment?

You ask for a hearing before the county Board of Supervisors, and the Chancery Clerk is the contact for the process. The Department of Revenue says an appeal normally must be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax is due.

Before filing, call the assessor's office with comparable sales or repair estimates in hand. If your home needs a new roof or has foundation damage, photographs and contractor quotes carry more weight than an opinion. The board reviews valuations, hears objections and adopts the rolls, which is why the August date matters.

Does homestead exemption matter when you sell a DeSoto County house?

Yes, because it lowers the bill the buyer inherits and it does not carry over automatically after a sale. Applications are filed with the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and the state says you do not have to reapply each year unless something changes, such as ownership or marital status.

People 65 or older, and people who are totally disabled and otherwise eligible, are exempt from taxes on the first $75,000 of true value, according to the Department of Revenue. Homestead is not allowed if the owner or spouse is out of compliance with state income tax laws or has a vehicle tagged outside the county of the home. A buyer who plans to live in the house should file in their first year, since missing April 1 means waiting for the next assessment year.

What do sellers in DeSoto County usually face?

Sellers here often deal with a mix of timing, repairs and carrying costs. A few patterns come up again and again:

  • Check that the owner name, mailing address and homestead status on the roll are current, since a bill sent to the wrong address is still due.
  • Inherited homes anywhere in the county can carry unpaid taxes or unrecorded paperwork that must be cleared before closing.
  • Rentals in Class II carry a higher assessment ratio, which matters to an investor selling a tenant-occupied house.
  • Newer subdivisions can sit in a city levy, while a house outside city limits does not, so two similar homes can have different bills.

A cash sale can shorten that list because the buyer purchases as-is and closes on a date you choose. You still need a clean title, a payoff for any mortgage and the current tax paid or settled on the closing statement. How do I check what I owe before selling?

Start with the county's online tax search, which lists real and personal property by name, parcel or address and shows amounts due. Then confirm with the collector by phone, since tax-sale and prior-year balances can appear separately.

  1. Find the parcel number on your deed or the assessor's lookup.
  2. Check the current and prior-year balances with the Tax Collector in Hernando or Olive Branch.
  3. Ask the Chancery Clerk whether any past sale exists on the parcel.
  4. Give your title company the figures so they can settle taxes at closing.

Where is Lowndes County, Mississippi?

Lowndes County is on Mississippi's eastern border with Alabama, and its county seat is Columbus. At the 2020 census it had 58,879 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 57,346, a decline of 2.6 percent. The county forms the Columbus micropolitan area and is one of three counties in the Golden Triangle region.

It covers 516 square miles, of which 506 are land and 11 are water. Its neighbors are Noxubee County to the south, Oktibbeha to the west, Clay to the northwest, Monroe to the north, and Lamar and Pickens counties in Alabama to the east. The land was fully wooded before settlement; the level areas are now cleared for farming or development, and the drainages, about 40 percent of the total area, remain wooded.

The Tennessee-Tombigbee Waterway runs through the center of the county, with the John C. Stennis Lock and Dam near Columbus. US 45, US 45 Alternate, US 82 and Mississippi Highways 12, 50, 69 and 182 are the main highways.

Which communities and school districts are in Lowndes County?

Columbus is the only city. The towns are Artesia, Caledonia and Crawford, and the census-designated places are Columbus Air Force Base and New Hope. Unincorporated communities include Bent Oak, Billups, Flint Hill, Forreston, Kolola Springs, Mayhew, McCrary, Penns, Plum Grove, Steens, Trinity, Wells, Whitebury and Woodlawn.

Two public systems serve the county. The Columbus Municipal School District runs Columbus High School, Columbus Middle School, the McKellar Technology Center and five elementary magnet schools. The Lowndes County School District has three areas, Caledonia, New Hope and West Lowndes, each with an elementary, middle and high school. Private options include Heritage Academy, Columbus Christian Academy, Victory Christian Academy and Annunciation Catholic School. The Mississippi University for Women is in Columbus.

School district boundaries matter to a property tax bill, since the state notes that county, municipal and school levies are combined in the millage rate.

What drives the Lowndes County economy?

Lowndes County combines manufacturing, a military base and a university. The Lowndes County Economic Development Commission lists American Colloid (bentonite clay), Bates Turkey Farm, Chowel Weldparts, Daehan Solutions Alabama, Findley Timber, Koch Foods, Priester Pecan, SABIC engineered plastics and Sejong Alabama among its top industries. The regional development group GTR Link says the Golden Triangle includes steel and metal, timber, aerospace, defense, automotive and technology companies.

Columbus Air Force Base, home of the 14th Flying Training Wing, sits about 8 miles north of downtown Columbus off Highway 45. Military One Source describes Columbus as a low-cost military town with many retirees.

The Golden Triangle Regional Airport completed a terminal expansion that added 8,200 square feet, according to a July 28, 2026 note from Congressman Trent Kelly.

If the size of your house was recorded wrongly, the state says a refund for prior years may be possible through the Chancery Clerk.

The assessor's staff can walk you through the value on the roll before you file. Take your photos, any recent appraisal and recent sales of similar houses with you.

What happens to unpaid Lowndes County taxes?

Delinquent property is sold at the county tax sale, and the owner has two years to redeem. A 2017 Commercial Dispatch report said Lowndes County moved its tax sale online that year through GovEase, with about 1,900 parcels carrying $1.6 million in delinquent taxes. The paper's report also said the owner who redeems pays the delinquent taxes and the buyer's money is returned with monthly interest, and that if two years pass the buyer can get a tax deed from the chancery clerk.

Those figures are old and the format may have changed, so ask the Tax Office for the current sale date. The state says sales can occur on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August. For land already sold to the state, call the Secretary of State at 1-866-835-2637.

For a Lowndes County homeowner, the simplest fix is to sell before the sale date. The title company pays the taxes from the proceeds.

Selling a Lowndes County house: what to line up

Selling in Lowndes County follows the same Mississippi steps as elsewhere: a title search, a prepared deed, payment of taxes and liens at closing, and recording with the chancery clerk.

  • Pull the parcel on the Property Link search to see the assessed value and tax status.
  • Ask the tax office for a payoff on any delinquent years.
  • Check homestead status, since an owner-occupied single-family home is assessed at 10 percent and other real property at 15 percent.
  • For inherited houses, the chancery court handles probate and the clerk files the papers.

Owners in Columbus, Caledonia, New Hope or the rural west of the county sometimes sell as-is because of repairs, a move for work, or an estate. How does the homestead exemption work for a Lowndes County home?

Homestead exemption applies to the house you live in and is filed with the tax assessor in the county where the home sits, between January 1 and April 1. You do not reapply each year, but you should refile if your marital status or ownership changes.

The Department of Revenue says homeowners 65 or older, and those who are totally disabled, can be exempt on the first $75,000 of true value if otherwise eligible. Harrison County has two county seats, Gulfport and Biloxi, and the county assessor runs a separate office in each judicial district. It was established on February 5, 1841, from parts of Hancock, Jackson and Perry counties, and it is named for President William Henry Harrison.

Wikipedia lists the total area as 976 square miles, of which 402 square miles (41%) is water, making it the second-largest county in Mississippi by total area. Two hurricanes define the county's building history: Camille on August 17, 1969, and Katrina on August 29, 2005, both of which Wikipedia describes as causing catastrophic damage. Hurricane Georges in 1998 also pushed the Tchoutacabouffa River over its banks near Old Highway 67 and Mississippi 15.

For a seller, that history shows up in questions a buyer asks first. Is the lot in a flood zone, was the house rebuilt after a storm, and is the roof recent? Ask your insurer and the county for the facts on your own parcel.

The county also has an older layer of history. The French built Fort Maurepas in 1699, hotels opened along the coast in the 1880s, and Keesler Field arrived in the early to mid 1900s. That mix explains why a Biloxi bungalow, a Long Beach cottage and a newer D'Iberville subdivision can have so little in common.

The owner has two years from the date of the tax sale to redeem, according to Mississippi Supreme Court opinions citing Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3. The Chancery Clerk must notify the owner of the sale and of the right to redeem.

Where is Jackson County, Mississippi, and is it the same as the city of Jackson?

No. Jackson County is on the Gulf Coast in the southeastern corner of Mississippi, about 190 miles from the state capital, and it has no relation to the city of Jackson in Hinds County. Its county seat is Pascagoula.

The county covers 1,043 square miles in total, of which 723 are land and 321 are water. That 31 percent water share makes it the largest county in Mississippi by total area. It borders George County to the north, Harrison and Stone counties to the west and northwest, and Mobile County, Alabama, to the east. The soil is sandy and the land sits in the Piney Woods region.

The cities are Gautier, Moss Point, Ocean Springs and Pascagoula. Unincorporated communities and census-designated places include Big Point, Escatawpa, Gulf Hills, Gulf Park Estates, Helena, Hurley, Latimer, St. Martin, Vancleave and Wade. Interstate 10 and US 90 are the main east-west roads, and several state highways, including MS 57, 63 and 609, run north.

Protected land is a big part of the map: parts of De Soto National Forest, Grand Bay National Wildlife Refuge and Gulf Islands National Seashore lie inside the county, along with the Mississippi Sandhill Crane National Wildlife Refuge.

Who runs property tax in Jackson County?

Jackson County keeps the tax assessor and the tax collector as two separate offices. The county's own site notes it is one of 17 Mississippi counties with separate assessor and collector offices.

What is the Jackson County property tax calendar?

Taxes are due by February 1, after being assessed to the owner of record as of January 1. The Mississippi Department of Revenue says bills go out in November or December, and a February 1 date that lands on a weekend or holiday moves to the next Monday without interest.

The Jackson County Tax Assessor's calendar lists April 1 as the deadline for homestead exemption, builder affidavits and business personal property renditions, and the first Monday in July as the date the rolls are presented. The Board of Supervisors begins hearing appeals on the first Monday in August, according to the county's appraisal page.

  • January 1: assessment date and ownership date.
  • April 1: homestead exemption and rendition filing deadline.
  • First Monday in July: rolls presented.
  • First Monday in August: appeals heard by the Board of Supervisors.
  • February 1: payment due date.

Late payment draws interest of one-half of one percent per month starting February 1, under Mississippi Code 27-41-9.

How do hurricanes affect Jackson County property tax and house sales?

Hurricane history is part of the county's property record. Jackson County was severely damaged by Hurricane Camille in August 1969 and Hurricane Katrina on August 29, 2005, and both caused catastrophic effects, according to the county's Wikipedia entry.

State law has a built-in relief valve for delays. Under Mississippi Code 27-41-9, the governor may extend the date for charging interest by proclamation when unusual conditions delay payment through no fault of the taxpayer or collector, by up to 60 days, with two further extensions possible. Separately, the state's tax agency has published a notice titled "Hurricane Katrina: Possible Property Tax Relief" that points to section 27-35-143(9), which lets boards of supervisors adjust assessments in certain circumstances. Ask the chancery clerk whether that section applies to your parcel.

For sellers, storm damage that is not yet repaired affects both value and financing. A house with roof or water damage may not pass a lender's inspection, which is one reason owners here sometimes sell as-is. If you think storm damage lowered your value, remember the appeal window closes on the first Monday in August.

How does the Jackson County economy affect housing?

Jackson County describes itself as the most industrialized county in Mississippi. The Jackson County Economic Development Foundation names Ingalls Shipbuilding as the state's largest employer, and lists Chevron, Fairbanks Morse, Bollinger Shipyards, Northrop Grumman and others among local employers.

The foundation reports an average manufacturing wage of $80,129, compared with $54,817 statewide, and a labor force above 68,000. It also says 8.5 percent of residents aged 18 to 64 are veterans. Healthcare employers include Singing River Health System, and the foundation works with Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College on training for the shipyard and refinery workforce.

Population has grown through recent decades: 118,015 in 1980, 143,252 in 2020 and an estimated 147,666 for 2025. Steady industrial employment tends to bring buyers who want to be near Pascagoula, Moss Point or Ocean Springs, while storm-exposed and older houses may take longer.

Which school districts serve Jackson County neighborhoods?

Four public districts divide the county. The Jackson County School District covers communities such as Hurley, Wade, Big Point, Three Rivers, Harleston, Vestry, Latimer and Vancleave, along with St. Martin and a small part of Escatawpa. Pascagoula-Gautier School District serves Pascagoula and most of Gautier, Moss Point School District serves Moss Point and most of Escatawpa, and Ocean Springs School District serves Ocean Springs.

Since municipal and school levies are part of the combined millage rate, the district where a house sits affects the tax bill as well as the school. The state explains that counties, municipalities and school districts each set their own levy, so two houses of the same value in different districts can owe different amounts.

What happens to unpaid Jackson County taxes?

Unpaid real estate tax makes the property subject to the county tax auction. The state says tax sales can be held on the first Monday in April and the last Monday in August, and that anyone with questions about a specific sale should contact the county tax collector.

Once a property is sold for taxes, the owner has two years from the sale date to redeem it by paying the delinquent taxes with statutory damages and interest, and the chancery clerk is supposed to notify the owner of that right. If nobody redeems, the buyer can receive a tax deed. For land sold to the state, the Secretary of State can be reached at 1-866-835-2637.

Selling a Jackson County house with taxes, liens or storm damage

A house can be sold with taxes owed, because the amount is found in the title search and paid out of the sale proceeds. The same approach works for liens and unpaid mortgage balances.

They are due by February 1 each year. If February 1 falls on a weekend or holiday, you may pay the next Monday without interest, and later payments carry one-half of one percent interest per month.

Payments go to the Jackson County Tax Collector at 2915 Canty Street in Pascagoula, or by mail to Box 998, Pascagoula, MS 39568. The phone number is 228-769-3074 and hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays.

The county's own demographics page lists nine communities: Brandon, Florence, Flowood, Pearl, Pelahatchie, Puckett, Richland, Sandhill and Star. Wikipedia reports a 2020 census population of 157,031, the fourth-most populous county in Mississippi, with Pearl as the largest city.

How did Rankin County change from farmland to suburbs?

Rankin County moved from a mostly agricultural economy to a heavily populated suburban county over the twentieth century. The Mississippi Encyclopedia describes the recent shift away from agriculture and notes that in 1960 farmers made up just 13 percent of the workforce, with nearly a quarter of workers in industry, mainly furniture and timber.

It also names two long-standing institutions in the county: the Piney Woods Country Life School, started in 1909, and the Mississippi State Hospital at Whitfield. The state moved the hospital there from Jackson in the 1920s, and the town took the name Whitfield for Rankin native Henry Whitfield, governor from 1924 to 1926.

The same source notes that the county sits next to Hinds County and its urban center of Jackson, and that Rankin had no urban population of its own in the early twentieth century. Its population reached almost 44,000 in 1970 and topped 69,000 a decade later, which is the growth that turned small towns such as Brandon, Pearl and Flowood into the communities listed above.

How does homestead exemption work in Rankin County?

You file for homestead exemption with the Rankin County Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1, and the first filing has to be made in person. According to the county's Filings and Exemptions page, the benefit renews automatically each year after that unless your filing status changes.

A new application is needed after these changes:

  • A change in ownership, use or occupancy.
  • Acquiring new property or a change in the property description.
  • Turning sixty-five or becoming 100% disabled for the first time.

The county warns that failing to tell the Tax Assessor about a change in homestead status may bring a fine of up to $5,000, two years in prison, or both. An owner who is 65 or older, or 100% disabled, is generally exempt on 160 acres or about $75,000 of appraised value, whichever limit is reached first. Anything over that is taxed.

Rankin County bills follow the state formula, which is true value times assessment ratio times the combined millage for your county, school district and, if you live in a city, that city. The state classes owner-occupied single-family homes at 10% of true value and other real property at 15%, per the Department of Revenue FAQ.

Code 25-7-9, effective January 1, 2020, posted by the Harrison County Chancery Clerk from the Mississippi Chancery Clerk's Association.

The recorder can add $10 for a document that does not meet the format rules in Miss. Code 89-5-24. Fees may change, so call the Rankin Chancery Clerk before sending a check. Our Mississippi quitclaim deed guide explains the format and recording rules.

Where is Lafayette County, Mississippi, and what is in it?

Lafayette County is in north Mississippi, and its county seat and largest municipality is Oxford. The 2020 census counted 55,813 residents. Locals pronounce the name "la-FAY-et."

The county covers 679 square miles, of which 632 are land and 47 are water. It borders Marshall, Union, Pontotoc, Calhoun, Yalobusha, Panola and Tate counties. Part of Holly Springs National Forest lies within it, and the Oxford micropolitan statistical area takes in the whole county.

Communities include Oxford, the towns of Abbeville and Taylor, the census-designated places of Paris, Tula and University, and unincorporated places such as Blackwater, Denmark, Harmontown, Springdale and Yocona. The county is often regarded as the inspiration for William Faulkner's fictional Yoknapatawpha County.

Main roads are US 278 and Mississippi Highways 6, 7, 9W, 30, 315, 331 and 334. The University of Mississippi is in the county, and Northwest Mississippi Community College runs the Lafayette-Yalobusha Technical Center. Public school districts are the Lafayette County School District and the Oxford School District.

Who handles property tax in Lafayette County?

One elected official, the Tax Assessor/Collector, does both jobs in Lafayette County. The office is at 300 N. Lamar Blvd., Suite 103, in Oxford. The tax collector line is 662-234-6006 and the assessor line is 662-234-5562, with a fax at 662-238-7992.

You can pay in the office, over the phone or online through Delta Computer Systems. The county accepts cash, credit card, money order, or a personal check when you show a driver's license and give a phone number. The county's Tax Assessor/Collector page has the links. The assessor is responsible only for assessing value and does not set the rate.

Oxford's city site also carries a link to pay property taxes online, so confirm with the city whether a house inside city limits gets a separate municipal bill.

How do I appeal a Lafayette County assessment?

Start with an informal review at the assessor's office, then file a formal appeal with the Board of Supervisors through the Chancery Clerk. The informal meeting is not yet an appeal. It checks your property record card, explains how the value was estimated, compares you with similar properties and screens you for exemptions.

If you still disagree, the formal appeal begins by contacting the Chancery Clerk at P.O. Box 1240, Oxford, MS 38655, with a copy to the Tax Collector/Assessor. The county says appeals are stronger when they show comparable properties assessed for less, and it calls a recent appraisal of your own property the best evidence.

The board looks only at fairness and accuracy, and the county says it is not interested in whether you can afford the tax. Foreclosures, short sales, bankruptcy sales, auctions and bank-owned homes are not treated as good sales in setting true values. That matters to anyone who sold at a discount, because that price will not feed into the neighbors' values.

What is the Lafayette County homestead exemption?

Homestead is a lower assessment ratio for the house you live in. A single-family home occupied by its owner with homestead is assessed at 10 percent of appraised value rather than 15 percent, and the application goes through the assessor.

The state says applications are due between January 1 and April 1, that you need not reapply each year unless your status changes, and that missing the April 1 date means no exemption for that assessment year. People 65 or older and those totally disabled, if otherwise eligible, are exempt on the first $75,000 of true value. The state also says a person can lose eligibility by not complying with state income tax law or by tagging a car in another county.

For a seller, homestead has a closing angle. The lower 10 percent ratio applies to an owner-occupied single-family home, so a buyer who will not live in the house may be assessed differently from the seller. Ask the assessor how a change of ownership is handled before you estimate the next bill.

How does the Lafayette County tax sale work?

Lafayette County holds its tax sale online at GovEase.com on the last Monday of August, from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. each day until all parcels are sold. Bidders register for free and must supply a Social Security or Tax ID number and a W-9, plus payment and a maximum bid.

The auction items are advertised twice in August in The Oxford Eagle. By law, overbids are settled to the county general fund, and a redeeming owner pays the original starting amount plus interest. The county states that if the owner does not redeem within two years after the purchase date, the purchaser can acquire the property by tax deed.

Land that was forfeited to the state can be purchased through the Public Lands Division, 601-359-6373, or toll free in Mississippi at 1-866-TFLANDS.

For an owner who has fallen behind on taxes, the practical point is that the clock starts at the sale, not at the bill. Selling before the last Monday in August lets the title company pay the taxes at closing.

What do sellers in Lafayette County deal with?

Lafayette County is a university county, with the University of Mississippi inside its borders and Oxford as the seat. Several things come up when owners sell here:

  • Rentals: a landlord selling a student rental may deal with a lease that runs past the closing date.
  • Inherited homes: probate matters are handled through the chancery court, and the Chancery Clerk's office is where heirs begin.
  • Delinquent taxes: balances are cleared from proceeds, and the Tax Collector/Assessor can supply a payoff figure.
  • Valuation disputes: the informal review and the first-Monday-in-August appeal date apply to your parcel whether you are selling or keeping.

How is a Lafayette County deed recorded?

The Chancery Clerk records deeds and keeps land records, and an assessor such as Hinds County's explains that it relies on filed deeds to keep ownership current. Hinds County's chancery clerk describes the usual sequence: a title search by an attorney or title company, then a deed with a notarized seller signature, a legal description and the parties' details, then recording. Ask Lafayette's clerk whether local requirements differ.

Because the state fixes ownership for assessment as of January 1, settle in the contract who pays the February 1 bill, and have the title company document it.

How is a Lafayette County tax bill calculated, and what is the penalty for paying late?

The state formula is true value times the assessment ratio times the millage rate, and each taxing body, meaning the county, a municipality and the school district, sets its own levy. The Department of Revenue gives a worked example: a $10,000 property at 15 percent has $1,500 of assessed value, and at 100 mills that is $150 of tax.

After February 1, interest of one-half of one percent per month, or fraction of a month, is added under Mississippi Code 27-41-9.

They are due by February 1 each year. Mississippi allows payment on the next Monday, without penalty, if February 1 falls on a weekend or legal holiday.

Does Lafayette County have a separate assessor and collector?

No. Lafayette County has one elected Tax Assessor/Collector at 300 N. Lamar Blvd., Suite 103 in Oxford. The assessor line is 662-234-5562 and the collector line is 662-234-6006.

What is the deadline to appeal a Lafayette County assessment?

The first Monday in August is the deadline to file with the Board of Supervisors. The board finalizes values on the third Monday in August, so schedule your informal review in July when the rolls are open.

When is the Lafayette County tax sale?

The online tax sale at GovEase.com starts on the last Monday of August. The owner has two years after the purchase date to redeem before the buyer can obtain a tax deed.

Can I sell a Lafayette County house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. Back taxes appear in the title search and are paid from the sale proceeds. If the house has already sold at the tax sale, the owner can still redeem within two years.

Hattiesburg and Petal are the two cities, and a small part of Hattiesburg lies across the line in Lamar County. Smaller places include Glendale, Rawls Springs, Brooklyn, Carnes and McLaurin. The three cities are Bay St. Louis, Diamondhead and Waveland. Kiln and Pearlington are census-designated places, and smaller communities include Lakeshore, Clermont Harbor, Necaise and Napoleon. How did Hurricane Katrina change Hancock County housing?

Katrina made its final landfall here on August 29, 2005, and the county's own history is the main reason local sellers talk about storm damage first. Wikipedia's county article reports that not one building or home was left intact along the 7-mile beach front, that nearly the entire first block off the beach was destroyed, and that homes as far as 10 miles inland flooded.

Highway 603 south of Interstate 10 was submerged and the Highway 90 bridge at Bay St. Louis was wrecked. Bay St. Louis, Waveland, Pearlington, Diamondhead and Kiln all took heavy damage. Ask any seller of a coastal house how it fared in 2005, because buyers will.
